The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergence by asking how nanoscale/1D sequence and epigenetic features give rise to stable 3D chromatin domains (TADs/loops) and epigenetic memory. Emergence is central to the framing, hypotheses, and planned analyses.

Feasibility would improve with narrower initial targets (few cell types/assays/resolutions) and explicit contingencies for compute and data heterogeneity.

Major repositories/consortia (ENCODE, 4D Nucleome, GEO) are identified, but specific datasets, inclusion/exclusion criteria, target cell types, assay versions, and resolutions are not specified. Limitations are acknowledged in general terms (noise/batch effects) but lack a concrete mitigation plan (QC thresholds, replicate handling, missing-modality strategies, cross-platform normalization).

The proposal commits to releasing code, trained models, and synthesized maps in public repositories and emphasizes reproducible workflows. It would be exemplary with more implementation detail (licenses, versioned pipelines/containers, data provenance, governance for team contributions, and a timeline for releases).

The scope is ambitious given the difficulty of harmonizing conditions across repositories and the computational burden of 3D EM segmentation plus RL modeling. Feasibility would improve with phased milestones (e.g., start with matched subsets, simpler predictive baselines) and explicit contingencies if cross-modal pairing is sparse.

Major repositories are clearly named (OpenOrganelle, Image Data Resource, Metabolomics Workbench), but specific datasets, inclusion criteria, and cross-dataset linkage plans are not specified. Limitations such as mismatched cell types/conditions, batch effects, imaging modality differences, and incomplete metadata are not adequately acknowledged or mitigated.

The proposal commits to open-source code and sharing derived network topologies and models via public platforms, aligning with reproducible science goals. It would be stronger with concrete implementation details (versioned workflows/containers, preregistered analysis plans, governance for contributions, and clear licensing/FAIR metadata for derived products).

The AI/RL components are ambitious and potentially high-risk without clearer baselines, evaluation metrics, and staged milestones. original_review_text:
The proposal explicitly frames EV biogenesis as a mesoscale emergent phenomenon linking nanoscale cargo clustering to macroscopic membrane budding and release. Emergence is central to the hypotheses, questions, and planned cross-scale modeling.

Integrating EV multi-omics with imaging/structural resources using GNNs and multimodal deep learning is innovative and could yield broadly useful principles and tools. However, the claims of “universal rules” and deterministic prediction may be overstated given EV heterogeneity and dataset biases.

The pipeline is logically staged (harmonization → network modeling → prediction → biophysical modeling), but key methodological details are under-specified (ground-truth labels, pairing of parent-cell and EV datasets, validation strategy, confounding control, and uncertainty quantification). The proposed coarse-grained MD component may be difficult to justify purely from heterogeneous public data without clearer parameterization and validation plans.

The scope is ambitious: harmonizing multi-omics across repositories, integrating imaging/structural data, training large models, and adding MD simulations plus interpretability. Feasible with strong project management and prioritization, but the proposal lacks concrete milestones, decision points, and contingency plans if key data linkages (cell↔EV pairing) are sparse.

The work is explicitly restricted to publicly available datasets and focuses on integration/synthesis across repositories and modalities, with no new experimental data generation. The planned outputs (harmonized datasets, models, workflows) align strongly with community-scale synthesis.

Major repositories are named (Vesiclepedia/EVpedia/ExoCarta, PRIDE, GEO, EMPIAR, PDB), but limitations are not treated in depth (EV isolation/annotation variability, contamination, batch effects beyond generic correction, missing metadata, uneven coverage across cell types/conditions, and scarcity of matched parent-cell/EV pairs). More explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria and bias/quality-control plans are needed.

The proposal commits to releasing pipelines, synthesized datasets, and models via GitHub/Zenodo and emphasizes reproducibility. It would be stronger with concrete implementation details (versioned containers, workflow managers, licensing, governance for contributions, and a plan for handling restricted/attribution-sensitive source datasets).

This proposal is strongly aligned with the call’s focus on mesoscale emergence and community-scale synthesis, using only public data to connect nanoscale cargo organization to EV budding and release. Its multidisciplinary integration of EV omics repositories with imaging/structural resources, coupled to modern GNN and multimodal learning approaches, is a clear strength and could produce valuable shared datasets, reusable workflows, and broadly applicable analytical methods.

Key weaknesses are feasibility and rigor details: the plan does not sufficiently specify how matched parent-cell/EV training pairs will be assembled, how labels and benchmarks will be defined, how confounders (isolation methods, contamination, cell-type imbalance, batch/metadata gaps) will be controlled, and how predictions will be validated and uncertainty quantified. The coarse-grained MD component, while conceptually appealing, needs clearer justification, parameterization strategy, and success criteria given heterogeneous public inputs. Tightening milestones, prioritizing a minimal viable set of questions/models, and adding explicit QC/validation and contingency plans would substantially strengthen the application.

original_review_text:
The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergence (viral inclusion bodies/factories) and explicitly frames the central problem as how microscale interactions scale to emergent compartments and cellular outcomes.

Cross-viral-family synthesis linking interactomes, spatial transcriptomics, and imaging with multimodal ML is ambitious and potentially high-impact, though similar network/AI integration paradigms exist and the proposal does not yet articulate a uniquely differentiating conceptual advance beyond “apply GNN/CV to integrated data.”

The pipeline is logically staged (harmonize → integrate → model), but key methodological details are underspecified (ground-truth labels for inclusion-body phenotypes, handling batch effects/confounding across studies, negative controls, validation strategy, and criteria for causal vs correlational claims).

Integrating heterogeneous interactome, spatial/single-cell transcriptomic, and imaging datasets across multiple viral families and training multimodal deep models is feasible but high-risk for a two-year working group without clearer milestones, prioritization, and contingency plans if key modalities lack matched metadata.

The work is explicitly and exclusively based on publicly available datasets and centers on integration/curation and synthesis analyses rather than generating new experimental data.

Major repositories are named (BioGRID/IntAct/STRING, GEO/ArrayExpress, IDR/EMPIAR, PDB, DisProt/MobiDB), but limitations are not treated in depth (incomplete/biased PPIs, variable infection conditions and timepoints, sparse spatial transcriptomics for many viruses, imaging annotation heterogeneity, and licensing/controlled-access constraints).

Commits to sharing code/workflows and integrated resources via public repositories and open-access publication, but lacks specifics on reproducibility implementation (versioned data releases, containers, workflow managers, governance for contributions, and handling of any restricted datasets).

This is a strong fit to the call: it squarely addresses mesoscale emergent phenomena (viral inclusion bodies) and proposes a community-scale synthesis that integrates multiple public data modalities to uncover generalizable principles of host-cell hijacking. The conceptual framing—linking local viral–host interactions to emergent mesoscale compartments and downstream cellular outcomes—is compelling, and the planned transdisciplinary collaboration and trainee involvement align well with NCEMS goals.

The main weaknesses are methodological specificity and feasibility risk. The proposal should more clearly define (i) which viruses/datasets will be prioritized, (ii) how inclusion-body phenotypes will be labeled/standardized from imaging, (iii) how cross-study confounding and batch effects will be controlled, (iv) what constitutes validation (e.g., held-out viruses/cell types, ablations, negative controls, benchmarking against simpler models), and (v) realistic milestones/contingencies if matched spatiotemporal imaging–omics data are scarce. Strengthening the data limitation analysis and providing a concrete open-science/reproducibility plan (containers, workflow orchestration, versioned releases, governance) would materially improve rigor and deliverability.

The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergence by linking molecular crowding to higher-order organization (condensates, compartmentalization, channeling) and explicitly frames threshold/nonlinear behaviors as emergent outcomes.

Integrating proteome-scale abundance, structure-derived volumes, spatial localization, and in vivo biophysics into a unified “crowding atlas” is highly novel and could substantially advance quantitative cell organization, though similar integrative efforts exist in adjacent resource-mapping domains.

The overall logic is sound (harmonization, uncertainty propagation, held-out validation), but key methodological risks are under-specified—especially comparability of diffusion/kinetics across assays, identifiability of compartment-level crowding from localization data, and validation without new experiments.

Three ambitious aims (atlas + literature-mined biophysics + agent-based models) across many organisms/conditions may be difficult in three years; feasibility would improve with sharper scoping (e.g., a few reference cell types) and explicit milestones/stop criteria.

The work is explicitly and exclusively based on integrating existing public datasets and published measurements, aligning strongly with community-scale synthesis expectations.

Major sources are clearly named (PaxDb/PRIDE, PDB/AlphaFold, HPA/OpenCell, LLPS and pathway/interaction databases), but limitations are not treated in depth (batch effects, inconsistent localization granularity, assay heterogeneity, missing negative results, and organism/cell-type mismatches).

The proposal commits to open databases, tools, and reproducible workflows (version control, containerization), but lacks concrete governance details (licensing, data provenance/redistribution constraints, preregistered analysis plans, and long-term maintenance commitments).

This is a strong fit to the call: it squarely addresses mesoscale emergent phenomena by synthesizing heterogeneous public data to connect crowding to condensates, spatial reaction organization, and non-additive biophysical effects. The planned deliverables (crowding atlas, predictive toolkit, and integrative models) are potentially high-impact community resources, and the multidisciplinary team structure aligns well with working-group goals and training aims.

Primary weaknesses are execution risk and underdeveloped treatment of data/measurement heterogeneity. The proposal would benefit from tighter scoping (defined reference organisms/cell types and a minimal viable atlas), clearer milestones and success metrics, and a more explicit strategy for harmonizing/normalizing biophysical measurements across modalities and conditions (including negative/contradictory findings). Strengthening the open-science plan with specific licensing, provenance tracking, and sustainability/maintenance pathways would further improve confidence in long-term community value.

The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergent behaviors driven by IDRs—especially phase separation/condensate formation and network-level signaling hub behavior—and explicitly frames these as emergent properties arising from sequence-encoded features.

Integrating sequence grammar, ensemble/structural descriptors, PTMs, interaction networks, and cellular context into unified predictive models is highly significant and likely to advance the field beyond current single-dataset or single-feature predictors, though similar integrative efforts exist in parts (e.g., LLPS predictors and motif resources).

The overall workflow is logical (database build → interaction mapping → emergent behavior prediction) and uses standard validation concepts, but key rigor elements are underspecified (label definitions, negative sets, leakage control across homologs, batch effects, and causal vs correlational interpretation across heterogeneous datasets).

The scope (50,000+ IDRs, multi-omics integration, web tools, multiple predictors, workshops) is ambitious for a 2-year effort with one coordinating postdoc and distributed trainees; achievable if narrowed to a few high-confidence organisms/datasets and prioritized deliverables, but risk of overextension is nontrivial.

Major data sources are clearly enumerated (e.g., DisProt/MobiDB/PED/BMRB/PhaSepDB/DrLLPS/LLPSDB/BioGRID/IntAct/PhosphoSitePlus/HPA/GTEx), but limitations are only lightly treated; stronger discussion is needed on annotation noise, LLPS ascertainment bias, context dependence of PTMs/PPIs, and inconsistent IDR boundary definitions across databases.

The proposal commits to public release of resources, documentation, and version-controlled workflows and mentions reproducible infrastructure, but lacks concrete implementation details (licenses, governance/maintenance plan, preregistered benchmarks, data provenance tracking, and long-term hosting/sustainability).

This is a strong fit to the call: it squarely addresses mesoscale emergent phenomena (LLPS/condensates and network-level regulation) and proposes a community-scale synthesis that integrates multiple public datasets spanning sequence, ensembles/structure, PTMs, interactions, and cellular context. Major repositories and data types are clearly identified (PRIDE/MassIVE/ProteomeXchange, GEO/ArrayExpress, PDB/AlphaFold, EMPIAR), but limitations are not fully developed (e.g., inconsistent SG isolation protocols, imaging metadata variability, negative controls, and cross-study comparability).

Methodological rigor would be improved by explicitly addressing batch effects and protocol heterogeneity, defining inclusion/exclusion criteria and negative controls, and describing how uncertainty will be quantified and propagated across modalities; open-science plans would benefit from more concrete implementation details for archiving, licensing, and long-term maintenance.

original_review_text:
The proposal directly targets metabolons as mesoscale, transient assemblies and explicitly frames substrate channeling and pathway-level behavior as emergent properties arising from collective molecular organization.

Integrating interaction, structure, localization, metabolomics, and fluxomics to derive cross-species principles of channeling is highly innovative and likely impactful, though similar integrative paradigms exist in other complex-assembly contexts.

The overall workflow is logical, but key inferential risks are under-specified (e.g., distinguishing true physical channeling from co-complex/co-localization, handling condition-specificity, and validating docking/AlphaFold-based assemblies without strong constraints).

The scope (multi-omics harmonization across five organisms plus docking/MD and phenotype modeling) is ambitious for three years; feasibility would improve with clearer prioritization of pathways, staged deliverables, and explicit go/no-go criteria for deep structural modeling.

The project is explicitly and exclusively based on publicly available datasets and focuses on integrating heterogeneous resources into new models and community deliverables without proposing new experimental data generation.

The proposal commits to public release of databases, models, and workflows and emphasizes reproducibility, but lacks concrete implementation details (licenses, versioned repositories, containerized pipelines, governance for curation, and timelines for releases).

This is a strong fit to the call: metabolons are a canonical mesoscale organization problem, and the proposal explicitly links transient enzyme assemblies to emergent pathway-level behavior. The planned synthesis across interaction resources, structural models, localization, metabolomics, and fluxomics—paired with cross-species comparisons—could yield valuable general principles and high-utility community resources (interaction database, structural/functional models), and it clearly requires multidisciplinary collaboration.

Feasibility would be improved by narrowing initial scope (specific pathways/organisms), adding staged milestones and contingency plans (e.g., when structural constraints are insufficient for reliable docking/MD), and providing a more detailed open-science implementation plan (versioned releases, containers, licensing, and curation governance).

The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergence by linking ribosome compositional heterogeneity to non-linear, system-level translational outcomes (the proposed “ribosome code”). The composition→structure→function framing explicitly operationalizes emergence across scales.

The project is explicitly and exclusively based on publicly available datasets (PDB/EMDB, GEO/SRA, PRIDE/MassIVE, MODOMICS/RMBase) and centers on integration rather than new experiments. Deliverables (atlas, models, predictors) are classic synthesis outputs.

The proposal explicitly frames the glycocalyx as a mesoscale structure whose collective organization yields emergent properties (barrier function, mechanosensing, immune recognition) not predictable from individual glycans. All three aims are organized around linking molecular composition/architecture to emergent cellular behaviors.

Integrating glycomics, glycoproteomics, structural resources, and functional phenotypes into an “Integrated Glycocalyx Atlas” and predictive models is a significant and timely synthesis effort in an under-integrated field. A three-year timeline for building a comprehensive atlas, mesoscale architecture models, and robust function-prediction tools is plausible but ambitious given heterogeneity and sparsity of public glycocalyx-relevant datasets. Feasibility would be stronger with explicit milestones, prioritization (e.g., a few cell types/contexts first), and contingency plans if key data types are missing or incompatible.

The project is explicitly restricted to publicly available datasets and centers on integrating multiple existing resources (GlyGen, GlyTouCan, UniCarb-DB, PDB/AlphaFold, ProteomeXchange/PRIDE, GEO/ArrayExpress). No new experimental data generation is proposed.

Major repositories are clearly named and relevant, and metadata standards (MIRAGE) are referenced. Nonetheless, limitations are not analyzed in sufficient depth (e.g., variable glycan annotation standards, incomplete linkage of glycans to protein carriers, organism/cell-type coverage gaps, and limited availability/standardization of functional assays).

The proposal commits to public release of databases, models, and workflows and describes reproducible practices (GitHub, Docker, shared environments). It would be exemplary with more concrete implementation details (licenses, governance/maintenance plan for the atlas, preregistered analysis plans, and explicit FAIR metadata/export formats).

This is a strong fit to the call: it squarely targets mesoscale emergence by asking how glycocalyx composition and 3D organization collectively generate higher-order cellular functions. The synthesis-only approach is clear and compelling, and the planned integration across glycomics, glycoproteomics, structural biology, and functional phenotypes—paired with community deliverables like an atlas and reusable pipelines—could substantially advance a fragmented field while enabling broad downstream hypothesis generation.

The main weaknesses are practical and methodological: the proposal underestimates the difficulty of harmonizing heterogeneous glycan annotations and quantitation across studies, controlling batch effects, and linking composition/architecture to functional outcomes in a way that is robust to confounding and missingness. Feasibility would improve with sharper scoping (initially focusing on a limited set of cell types/assays), explicit milestones and success metrics per aim, and contingency plans for sparse or incompatible data. original_review_text:
Enhancer–promoter specificity is framed explicitly as a mesoscale emergent property arising from integrated chromatin architecture, TF binding, chromatin state, and sequence features, aligning tightly with the call’s emergence focus.

While individual components (Hi-C integration, TF/mark features, ML prediction) are established, the proposed community-scale synthesis across modalities and cell types to derive generalizable “specificity rules” is significant and likely to advance the field.

The plan includes multi-caller consensus for loops, standardized reprocessing, matched negative controls, cross-cell-type validation, and interpretability (SHAP), but key risks (batch effects, label noise/ground truth ambiguity, and confounding by distance/TAD structure) are not fully mitigated with explicit sensitivity analyses.

Integrating and uniformly processing terabyte-scale Hi-C/Capture-C/HiChIP plus hundreds of ChIP-seq factors across many cell types, then building multiple model classes, is ambitious for three years without clearer phased milestones and down-selection criteria for cell types/factors.

The project is explicitly restricted to publicly available datasets and centers on integration/meta-analysis across distinct data types, fitting the definition of a synthesis working group.

Major sources (ENCODE, Roadmap, GTEx, 4DN, GEO) and data types are clearly identified, but limitations are only implicitly addressed; more explicit discussion is needed on uneven cell-type matching, assay resolution differences, replicate scarcity, and biases across consortia.

They commit to public release of databases, models, and reproducible workflows with containerization and workflow managers, but lack specifics on governance (authorship/credit), timelines for release, licensing, persistent identifiers, and a concrete reproducibility checklist.

This is a strong fit to the program’s emergence mission: enhancer–promoter specificity is a well-motivated mesoscale phenomenon, and the proposal’s central contribution is a community-scale synthesis integrating 3D genome contacts with chromatin state, TF binding, accessibility, expression, and eQTL evidence. The planned outputs (standardized connection atlas, interpretable predictive models, and a catalog of specificity rules) would be broadly useful and could materially improve how the field prioritizes regulatory links and interprets noncoding variation.

Primary weaknesses are feasibility and risk management. The scope (100+ cell types, hundreds of TF ChIP-seq datasets, multiple conformation assays, and several modeling paradigms) is likely to strain a three-year working group unless the team defines explicit phased milestones, criteria for selecting a core set of cell types/assays, and contingency plans when matched datasets are unavailable. Methodologically, the approach is generally rigorous, but would benefit from more explicit handling of batch effects and “ground truth” uncertainty in defining positive/negative enhancer–promoter pairs (e.g., sensitivity analyses across callers/resolutions, alternative labeling schemes, and confounder controls beyond distance matching). Open science intentions are strong but should be operationalized with clearer release timelines, licensing, and team governance.

original_review_text:
The proposal targets how mesoscale 3D genome architecture and chromatin state give rise to emergent, cell-type-specific transcriptional programs and disease-associated states in brain cells. Emergence is central, though the mechanistic link is framed largely through predictive modeling rather than explicit causal tests.

Integrating single-cell Hi-C with gene expression via multimodal transformer/contrastive learning is innovative and could materially advance understanding of structure–function relationships and neurodegenerative dysregulation. However, similar multimodal representation-learning paradigms exist, and the incremental novelty depends on execution and availability of suitable data.

The modeling concept is plausible, but key methodological details are underspecified (e.g., resolution/windowing of Hi-C matrices, batch correction strategy, evaluation metrics/baselines, and how bulk ATAC will be reconciled with single-cell targets). The plan also relies on strong assumptions about transferability from non-brain co-assays and cell-type-level alignment that may confound biological interpretation.

Building, pretraining, and validating a large multimodal generative model across disparate single-cell Hi-C and scRNA resources is ambitious, especially given stated lack of human brain co-assay data. Feasibility would improve with clearer milestones, smaller initial deliverables, and explicit fallback datasets/benchmarks.

The work is positioned as a synthesis/integration effort using existing public single-cell genomics datasets and developing reusable analytical tools, with no new experimental data proposed. The integration across modalities and studies is central to the project.

Data sources are described generically (e.g., 'datasets from Alzheimer’s patients,' 'single-cell Hi-C for various human brain tissues') without naming specific repositories, accessioned datasets, sample sizes, modalities, or coverage/resolution constraints. Limitations are acknowledged (scarce co-assays), but the implications for training/validation and confounding (batch, donor, protocol, sparsity) are not thoroughly analyzed.

The proposal does not provide concrete open-science plans (e.g., preregistered analysis plan, public code repositories, containerized workflows, data provenance, licensing, or governance for team science). It implies tool development but lacks explicit commitments aligned with the call’s open, reproducible, community policies.

This proposal addresses a compelling emergent-phenomena question: how mesoscale 3D genome organization and chromatin state collectively produce robust, cell-type-specific transcriptional programs in the brain and how these programs shift in Alzheimer’s disease. Rigor would be strengthened by explicit dataset lists and inclusion criteria, clear evaluation metrics and baselines, a validation strategy that separates biological signal from technical effects, and a more realistic phased scope. strengths: The proposal demonstrates strong scientific merit by targeting emergent mesoscale organization of mRNPs and integrating heterogeneous datasets into transcriptome-wide maps. weakness: Key weaknesses include the ambitious scope and timeline, which appear overly large for the proposed duration. original_review_text:
The proposal explicitly targets emergent mesoscale organization of mRNPs into higher-order interaction networks and biomolecular condensates, framing these as emergent behaviors arising from multicomponent interactions.

Integrating heterogeneous RNA–protein/RNA–RNA/PPI datasets into transcriptome-wide mRNP maps and linking them to condensate partitioning is highly innovative and could yield broadly useful resources, though parts (e.g., K562 focus, use of existing databases) are evolutionary rather than fully transformative.

The overall workflow is logical, but key methodological details are underspecified (e.g., concrete linked features, batch-effect handling, uncertainty propagation, and validation strategy beyond β-actin), and the MD-to-neural-network plan risks model mismatch without clearer calibration/benchmarking.

Delivering a robust multi-modal integration framework, a high-confidence K562 mRNP atlas, mesoscale community detection, residue-level simulations for ~2,500 mRNPs, and cross-cell-type stress granule predictions within 2 years appears overly ambitious given compute, curation, and validation demands.

The project is primarily based on integrating existing public datasets and databases, consistent with synthesis goals, though the proposed large-scale molecular dynamics simulations constitute substantial new derived data generation that may stretch the spirit of “only existing data.”

Some sources are named (e.g., CD-Code, RNA Granule Database, proximity labeling and crosslinking MS datasets), but major RNA–protein modalities (eCLIP/iCLIP/PAR-CLIP/RIP-seq, Ribo-seq, structure probing, etc.) are not explicitly enumerated and limitations (cell-type mismatch, condition dependence, assay biases) are not thoroughly analyzed.

They commit to open-source tools, public databases, and reproducible workflows, but the proposal lacks concrete implementation details (governance, licensing, versioned pipelines/containers, data provenance, and a clear plan for releasing large intermediate artifacts like simulation outputs).

This is a compelling, highly relevant proposal for mesoscale emergent phenomena, aiming to synthesize fragmented RNA–protein interaction evidence into transcriptome-wide mRNP maps and then connect those maps to higher-order organization such as stress granules and P bodies. The conceptual integration across nano- to mesoscale organization is a major strength, and the planned outputs (tools, atlases, and predictive models) could become valuable community resources if executed well.

Key weaknesses are feasibility and methodological specificity. The scope—especially residue-resolution simulations for thousands of mRNPs plus multi-modal integration, benchmarking, and cross-cell-type predictions—appears too large for a 2-year working group without clearer prioritization, staged milestones, and contingency plans. Rigor would be improved by explicitly listing target datasets/modalities, detailing normalization and uncertainty handling across assays, expanding validation beyond a single exemplar (β-actin), and clarifying how simulation-derived features will be calibrated to experimental condensate partitioning data to avoid overfitting or biophysical mismatch.

original_review_text:
The proposal targets how ensembles of intrinsically disordered regions encode sensing/adaptation across environments, which is an emergent property of sequence-to-ensemble behavior, but the mesoscale/cellular emergence framing (e.g., condensates, network-level regulation) is not explicit or central.

Systematically linking IDR biophysical ensemble properties to ocean-scale environmental gradients using metagenomics plus simulation/ML is highly original and could yield broadly useful principles and resources for IDR biology and protein engineering.

The pipeline is ambitious and logically staged, but key methodological risks are under-specified (metagenomic protein calling/quality control, orthology assignment, uncertainty propagation from structure/IDR predictors, and validation strategies for ML-derived adaptation claims).

The planned scale (tens of millions of proteins, AlphaFold/ESMFold annotation, and ~440,000 MD trajectories plus deep learning) appears difficult to complete in 24 months even with NCEMS support, and contingencies/prioritization criteria are not clearly defined.

The project primarily synthesizes existing public resources (Tara/Ocean Gene Atlas, OceanDNA, environmental metadata) and integrates them with computational annotations and simulations; however, the plan also mentions experimental testing via collaborations, which could conflict with an "existing data only" requirement unless explicitly excluded from funded scope.

Major data sources are named (OGA2/Tara Oceans, OceanDNA) and some limitations are acknowledged (ALBATROSS trained at physiological conditions; no pressure model), but additional critical limitations are not addressed (assembly/annotation biases, uneven sampling across depths/regions, taxonomic confounding, and uncertainty in predicted structures/IDRs for metagenomic proteins).

The proposal implies public release of a database and tools, but it lacks concrete implementation details (repositories, licensing, workflow provenance/containers, preregistered analysis plans, governance for team contributions, and reproducibility standards for large-scale simulations/ML).

This is a compelling, multidisciplinary synthesis concept that could produce a valuable community resource (a marine IDR catalog linked to environmental metadata) and generate new principles connecting IDR sequence chemistry to ensemble behavior across natural gradients. The integration of metagenomic context with biophysical simulation and representation learning is innovative and well aligned with community-scale data synthesis, with clear potential impact in evolutionary biophysics and protein design.

The main weaknesses are feasibility and rigor at scale: the proposal under-specifies quality control, orthology/functional context assignment, uncertainty quantification, and validation of inferred adaptation mechanisms, while the computational workload (structure prediction plus hundreds of thousands of trajectories and deep learning) appears unlikely to be completed within 24 months without sharper scoping and prioritization. Open-science plans should be made more concrete, and the team should explicitly clarify that no new experimental data generation is part of the funded work (or clearly separate any optional external validation).

The proposal explicitly addresses emergent phenomena at the mesoscale by investigating how the conformational dynamics and ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDRs) adapt to environmental gradients.

Combining global marine metagenomics with large-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics and deep learning to map IDR environmental adaptation is a groundbreaking approach with transformative potential for evolutionary and synthetic biology.

The methodology is highly detailed, logical, and integrates state-of-the-art tools (ESMFold, ALBATROSS, LAMMPS). The approach is rigorous, though the sheer scale of the computational pipeline introduces some complexity.

While the project is well-planned, generating and curating 440,000 molecular dynamics trajectories within an 11-month window is extremely ambitious and poses significant computational and data management challenges.

The project is strongly synthesis-focused, relying heavily on existing Tara Oceans data. However, the brief mention of experimental testing of de novo designs slightly deviates from the strict 'no new experimental data' mandate.

Data sources (Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0, OceanDNA) are explicitly and comprehensively identified. The proposal also thoughtfully acknowledges limitations, such as the lack of validated coarse-grained models for pressure.

The proposal demonstrates a strong commitment to open science by planning the public release of tools, datasets, and databases, though it lacks a highly detailed framework regarding specific FAIR repositories.

This proposal presents a highly innovative and scientifically rigorous plan to synthesize massive public metagenomic datasets (Tara Oceans) with biophysical simulations and machine learning. Furthermore, while the project is predominantly a data synthesis effort, the inclusion of experimental testing for de novo designed sequences borders on generating new experimental data, which conflicts slightly with the funding call's strict synthesis mandate. Finally, expanding on the specific open science frameworks and repositories to be used would further strengthen the proposal.

original_review_text:
The proposal directly targets mesoscale cellular organization as an emergent outcome of multicomponent interactions and physical constraints, using the nucleus-centered systems as explicit exemplars of emergence.

Integrating multicomponent imaging with in vitro and in silico datasets via Gromov-Wasserstein-based transfer learning and mutual prediction is innovative and could enable new cross-modal inference of mesoscale principles, though similar alignment ideas exist in adjacent single-cell/multimodal fields.

The overall logic (feature extraction → GW alignment → predictive modeling) is coherent, but key methodological details are underspecified (ground-truth definitions, validation strategy across datasets, handling batch effects/domain shift, uncertainty quantification, and failure modes for GAN-based inference).

A two-year plan spanning three biological systems, multiple modalities, GW computation at scale, and deep-learning model development is plausible but ambitious, with feasibility hinging on data availability/quality and substantial engineering for scalable GW and robust cross-dataset harmonization.

The intent is strongly synthesis-oriented, but the proposal explicitly mentions developing new simulations to close gaps, which risks drifting beyond an 'existing data only' synthesis scope unless constrained to reanalysis of already-published simulation outputs.

Data sources are described at a high level (e.g., multicomponent imaging, fibroblast HGPS datasets, published simulations) without naming specific repositories/datasets, inclusion criteria, or harmonization plans; limitations are acknowledged generally but not analyzed in a dataset-specific way.

The proposal states intent to produce open-source workflows and integrated datasets, but lacks concrete implementation details (repositories, licensing, preregistration/analysis plans, reproducible environments/containers, governance for team science, and data-sharing constraints for large images).

This proposal is strongly aligned with the call’s emphasis on emergent mesoscale phenomena, aiming to extract general principles of cellular organization by integrating multicomponent imaging with biophysical measurements and simulations. The conceptual innovation—using Gromov-Wasserstein alignment to enable transfer learning and mutual prediction across incomplete datasets—could be impactful for community-scale reuse of existing imaging resources and for generating testable hypotheses about component interactions.

Key weaknesses are (i) insufficient specificity about which public datasets will be used and how they will be curated/harmonized, (ii) methodological under-specification around validation, robustness to domain shift, and uncertainty, and (iii) potential noncompliance with the “no new data generation” requirement due to plans for new simulations. Strengthening the proposal would require enumerating concrete datasets/repositories, defining strict synthesis-only boundaries (e.g., limiting to published simulation outputs), and providing a clearer reproducibility and open-science execution plan (code/data release, containers, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics).

original_review_text:
Allostery is an archetypal emergent mesoscale phenomenon arising from collective, long-range coupling of residue motions and energy landscapes. The proposal explicitly targets emergent communication properties (strength, directionality, timescale) as system-level order parameters.

Deriving physically interpretable, comparable “order parameters” and an allostery score across proteins by integrating MD, DMS, and evolution is a notably innovative synthesis direction with broad potential impact. However, the claim of proteome-wide generalization and engineering is ambitious relative to the evidence provided for transferability.

The overall workflow is logical (MD-derived dynamic descriptors + DMS functional effects + evolutionary features + manifold learning/ML), but key methodological details are underspecified (descriptor definitions, validation metrics, uncertainty quantification, and controls for MD force-field/sampling bias). The plan also mixes multiple modeling paradigms (linear response, Bayesian inference, manifold learning) without clearly stating decision criteria and benchmarking strategy.

The 2-year plan spans large-scale MD generation (including new simulations), multi-dataset integration across ~28 proteins, model development, evolutionary analyses, and experimental validation, which is likely over-scoped. The requested 200 TB storage and heavy GPU hours further suggest substantial computational burden without clear contingencies for incomplete MD sampling or heterogeneous DMS assay comparability.

While the project strongly leverages public DMS (MaveDB) and public MD repositories, it also proposes generating substantial new MD trajectories and conducting new experimental tests, which moves beyond a pure synthesis working group. The core scientific aims could be synthesis-driven, but the current plan relies materially on new data generation.

Major sources are named (MaveDB, MDRepo, MDVerse; plus structure generation via AlphaFold/Boltz2/BioEmu), and the existence of a target list is indicated. However, limitations are not treated in depth (cross-assay normalization of DMS phenotypes, ligand-state metadata consistency, MD protocol heterogeneity, sampling adequacy, and bias introduced by predicted structures).

The proposal states intent to release tools (AllosteryMap) and curated datasets in public repositories, aligning with open science goals. Concrete implementation details are limited (versioned workflows, containerization, provenance/metadata standards, licensing, preregistered benchmarks, and governance for team contributions).

This proposal targets a compelling emergent phenomenon—protein allostery—and aims to formalize it via quantitative, physically interpretable order parameters derived from integrated public datasets (MD, DMS, and evolutionary sequences). The conceptual framing is strong and potentially impactful: a transferable “allostery score” and dynamic coupling descriptors could unify disparate case studies and enable comparative analyses across proteins and lineages.

Key weaknesses are feasibility and alignment with a strict synthesis-only working group model. The plan depends on generating substantial new MD simulations and includes new experimental validation, and the overall scope (proteome-scale classification, evolutionary scaling, tool building, and experimental design/validation within 2 years) appears over-ambitious. Methodological rigor would be improved by specifying descriptor definitions, benchmarking/validation protocols (including negative controls and uncertainty quantification), and explicit strategies for harmonizing heterogeneous DMS readouts and MD protocols. Strengthening the open-science plan with concrete reproducibility and data-governance practices would also increase competitiveness.

original_review_text:
The proposal targets emergence of complex protein topologies (knots/lassos) from sequence evolution and folding constraints, which is an emergent structural phenomenon, but links to mesoscale cellular emergence (networks/phenotypes) are secondary rather than central.

Mapping topological state changes onto phylogenies across many families using integrated topology/structure/functional resources is innovative and could yield broadly useful evolutionary principles and predictors of entanglement.

The overall workflow is logical, but key methodological details are under-specified (orthology/paralogy handling, topology-calling uncertainty, phylogenetic model choices, and statistical controls for confounding/annotation bias).

The ambition (29 families, ~300k sequences, multi-database overlays, and branch-point structure modeling) is high for 24 months; success seems plausible if narrowed to fewer exemplar families and if compute/curation bottlenecks are managed.

The project is primarily integrative, leveraging multiple public databases and tools to synthesize sequence/structure/topology/functional annotations; however, planned de novo structure prediction at branch points blurs the 'existing data only' boundary.

Data sources are clearly enumerated (UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold DB, KnotProt/LassoProt, OMA, TimeTree, etc.), but limitations are not thoroughly addressed (AlphaFold/topology false positives, uneven taxonomic sampling, viral data access constraints, and annotation incompleteness).

The proposal gestures toward an open, data-driven platform but lacks concrete plans for repositories, licensing, reproducible workflows (containers/notebooks), versioned releases, and governance for team science outputs.

This is a compelling synthesis concept that leverages the rapidly expanding ecosystem of topology annotations (KnotProt/LassoProt/AlphaKnot/AlphaLasso) together with orthology and divergence-time resources to pinpoint when complex protein entanglements emerged and how they relate to sequence features and functional hotspots. The cross-database integration and the focus on evolutionary “turning points” are strong and could produce broadly reusable phylogenetic/topological maps and hypotheses about adaptive value.

Key weaknesses are (i) insufficient methodological specificity for robust phylogenetic inference and statistical testing (e.g., controlling for family size, taxonomic sampling, structural coverage, and correlated annotations), (ii) an ambitious scope that risks overextension, and (iii) limited articulation of open-science implementation. The proposal would be strengthened by a tighter initial scope with explicit success metrics, a clear uncertainty/validation framework for topology calls (including AF confidence and topology tool agreement), and a detailed reproducibility plan (public code/data releases, workflow automation, and clear handling of restricted datasets such as GISAID).

The MD component is ambitious and risks limited rigor without clear sampling plans, selection criteria for simulated subsets, and benchmarking against experimental ensemble data.

The plan to curate ~1,500 IDRs, run large-scale alignments, build ML models, and perform extensive explicit-solvent all-atom MD (requesting 1,000,000 GPU hours) within 24 months is likely over-scoped. The project is explicitly a synthesis effort using only publicly available resources (UniProt, ELM, IDRome/MobiDB, MaveDB/ProteinGym, PTM databases, orthology resources, GISAID) and focuses on integration rather than new experiments. Outputs are framed as a community resource and integrative analyses.

Major data sources are clearly named and alternatives are provided, with some acknowledgment of incompleteness and bias in functional annotations. However, limitations around IDR alignment reliability, motif false positives from ELM predictions, PTM context dependence, and GISAID reuse constraints are not fully analyzed or mitigated with concrete QC/validation plans.

The proposal commits to an open-access database, reproducible workflows, and NCEMS/CyVerse-based dissemination, aligning well with open and team science expectations. It would be stronger with explicit details on licensing, versioning, governance/maintenance, containerized workflows, and how restricted datasets (e.g., GISAID) will be handled to ensure reproducibility.

This is a strong synthesis-centered proposal addressing an important and timely problem: how intrinsically disordered regions encode conserved function despite rapid sequence evolution. Its main strengths are the clear integration of multiple public resources (motifs, PTMs, DMS, disorder annotations, orthology) and the deliverable of a curated, open database that could materially improve IDR functional annotation and hypothesis generation. The primary weakness is feasibility and methodological specificity. original_review_text:
Allostery is an emergent, mesoscale phenomenon linking distributed residues, conformational ensembles, and function, and the proposal explicitly targets determinants and evolution of this system-level behavior in transporters.

Creating an 'augmented allosterome' with explicit negative/weak-allostery cases and using transporter family comparisons is a meaningful advance over existing allostery databases and could yield broadly useful predictive principles.

The overall workflow (curation → comparative sequence/structure/dynamics analyses → prediction) is logical, but key operational definitions (e.g., using domain insertion as a proxy for allostery) and validation plans for labels/predictions are not sufficiently specified to ensure robust inference.

The plan combines large-scale curation across ~50 families with extensive new MD (100–200 models, 20 ns each) and multiple ML efforts within 24 months, which is ambitious and risks being bottlenecked by labeling/annotation and compute-intensive simulations.

The project strongly emphasizes integrating public databases and literature, but it also proposes substantial new MD simulations/trajectory generation, which moves it away from a purely synthesis-only effort as described in the call.

Key sources (ASD, TCDB, MAVEdb, UniProt, InterPro, PDB) are clearly identified and major limitations (lack of negatives, sparsity, deprecated resources, labeling ambiguity) are acknowledged with a proposed workaround.

They commit to releasing the augmented database and products via CyVerse/NCEMS, but do not provide concrete implementation details (repositories, licensing, versioning, provenance, reproducible workflows/containers, governance for community augmentation).

This proposal targets a compelling emergent phenomenon—protein allostery—and aims to advance the field by synthesizing disparate public resources into an augmented transporter-focused allostery database that includes negative/weakly allosteric cases. The comparative framing across homologs, coupled with sequence coevolution, structural descriptors, and interpretable ML, has strong potential to yield generalizable principles about the determinants and evolutionary origins of allostery.

Primary weaknesses are feasibility and alignment with a strict synthesis-only scope. The planned scale of curation plus extensive new MD trajectory generation and multiple ML model comparisons appears overly ambitious for two years and introduces risk that the project becomes dominated by new computation rather than integration/analysis of existing public datasets. The proposal would be strengthened by (i) a clearer, experimentally grounded labeling rubric for allostery vs non-allostery beyond domain insertion proxies, (ii) explicit validation/benchmarking plans and success metrics, (iii) a staged scope with a smaller initial set of families and contingency paths if data are sparse, and (iv) a more detailed open-science and reproducibility plan (workflow tooling, containers, metadata/provenance, and governance for community contributions).

original_review_text:
The proposal targets how collective conformational ensembles and multi-timescale dynamics relate to enzyme function, which is plausibly emergent at the mesoscale, but it does not explicitly frame or test emergent phenomena as a central biological question.

Integrating multi-resolution MD trajectories with foundation-model embeddings via spatiotemporal GNNs and gated fusion is innovative and could materially advance function prediction beyond static sequence/structure paradigms.

The modeling pipeline is described clearly, but key rigor elements are underdeveloped (e.g., leakage control across homologs/structures, uncertainty calibration, causal claims for determinants, and robust baselines/ablation plans across simulation types and lengths).

Simulating 10,000 enzymes to 3 µs each and extracting extensive determinants within 24 months is likely unrealistic given the stated staffing and the heavy compute/storage/QA burden, even with CG and AI-MD acceleration.

While the project integrates multiple public datasets, it also proposes substantial new MD (CG and AI-MD) generation at large scale, which conflicts with an 'existing publicly available data only' synthesis requirement.

Major sources are explicitly named (UniProt/SwissProt, PDB, ATLAS, mdCATH, Anton/PSC, MARTINI, MDGen) and some limitations are noted (sampling/force-field issues), though dataset inclusion criteria and bias/coverage limitations are not fully analyzed.

The proposal commits to depositing processed trajectories/features and releasing workflows via open repositories (e.g., MDRepo, Zenodo, GitHub) and to open-access publication, but lacks concrete reproducibility details (versioned pipelines, containers, governance, licensing, and metadata standards).

This proposal has strong scientific promise: it tackles an important limitation of current protein function predictors by incorporating conformational ensembles and temporal information from MD, and the multi-modal architecture (spatiotemporal GNN + causal attention + multi-resolution fusion) is a compelling and potentially high-impact methodological contribution. The team composition is appropriately multidisciplinary, and the plan to benchmark against state-of-the-art predictors and release data/products aligns well with community utility.

However, there are two major weaknesses relative to the call. First, the project appears to rely heavily on generating new MD trajectories at very large scale (10,000 proteins, multi-microsecond targets), which undermines the synthesis-only requirement and also raises feasibility concerns for a 24-month working group with limited staff support. Second, several aspects of methodological rigor need strengthening, including explicit controls against train/test leakage across homologs and structures, clearer validation of claimed “causal” biophysical determinants, and a more detailed ablation/benchmarking and uncertainty strategy. A revised scope emphasizing integration of existing public MD repositories (with smaller, well-justified targeted additions if allowed) and a tighter emergent-phenomena framing would substantially improve responsiveness to the RFP.

[Scientific Merit and Innovation | Score: Not provided]
IDRs have long been thought to be protein-protein interaction hubs, and so the proposal that this can be quantified in terms of network organization doesn't seem particular innovative.   The focus on marginally stable proteins is perhaps more innovative, but the knoweldge gap is still not clearly articulated.

[Feasibility | Score: Not provided]
The details in the proposal are not sufficient for determining feasibility. There are still large knowledge gaps, e.g. about how mutations affect IDP-binding interactions that were not carefully considered

[Data Sources and Limitations | Score: Not provided]

[Open Science Compliance | Score: Not provided]
Not particular discussed, so not clear.

[Overall Rating | Score: Not provided]
The proposal aims to determine how unstable or intrinsically disordered proteins interface with protein-protein network topology.  The role of chaperones as secondary points of connectivity, as well as of the unique role in these proteins types in their promiscuity are all interesting questions. 

However, the details and connections between the aims lead to some concerns about the approach.  For example, proteins of marginal stability, according to the text, can be made more or less stable with single point mutations, but structure prediction is often relatively insensitive to mutation.  The overall argument feels a bit circular, that is IDPs that are more promiscusous are expected to be more promiscuous.  How do the authors propose to determine which IDRs are more promiscucous, other than the degree of connectededness in the networks, arising from (I presume) protein-protein interaction databases.  The evolutionary models given for folded proteins aren't clearly adaptable to intrinsically disordered proteins, or at least absent models of binding interactions, I'm not sure how to quantify mutational affects on binding affinity.  Moreover, proteins tend to be organized into domains, with few proteins being fully disordered or fully ordered.  It's unclear if the authors have considered even how to define a disordered protein, and that the degree of disorder may be variable.

original_review_text:
[Scientific Merit and Innovation | Score: Not provided]
The proposal aims to use the knowledge on intrinsically disordered proteins (IDP) and extend it to the proteins that do not manage to fold correctly in vivo (defined as “intrinsically unstable” forms – which the abstract states represent 10% of all proteins - citation?). The investigators propose to use network analysis AI assisted tools and various databases of protein stability and genes. The main hypothesis is that IDPs  play an important role in network communication while in their unstructured form, which drives the need of the investigators to make a connection between IDPs and intrinsically unstable forms of otherwise structured proteins. The major weakness of this proposal seems to come from the difficulty to assess for a given protein how much of the expressed molecules are intrinsically unstable. In the database table, I could only find one reference to assess protein stability - ProThem (source ID 7) – which also does not seem to provide the needed information. However, assuming that the PIs identify a folding/stability free energy database (which is also used as input in the P_native formula), it is not clear how the thermal stability of proteins measured in vitro, in the absence of any chaperones, can be related to propensity of a protein to be in an “intrinsically unstable” form in vivo, where chaperones help with folding.

[Feasibility | Score: Not provided]
Timeline is appropriate. However, the provided technical details are insufficient. For example, it is not clear how evolutionary models will be fine-tuned. More specific, from the definition of P_native, if a protein and chaperone do not interact (gamma=0), the formula produces a value of 0.5, which seems incorrect to me, and I could not find in the references cited an explanation on this. Does this mean on average, in the absence of chaperones, proteins have 0.5 probability to fold in their native form?
AI based models will have the natural tendency to predict the stable structures as they are occurring with higher probability, and it is not clear how the PIs intend to bias them for the  “intrinsically unstable” forms. How will they even be trained, given that there are no structure of the unstable forms? Is there a way to assess these predictions experimentally? Maybe knocking-out a protein from a “party hub”?

The proposal justifies the synthesis focus. However, some libararies do not seem to be correctly referenced and there is limited discussion on the shortcomings of the selected data bases

[Open Science Compliance | Score: Not provided]
The proposal does not seem to address this point.

[Overall Rating | Score: Not provided]
Trying to connect protein instability with their role in the interaction network is an interesting idea. However, there are some concerns on the currently available information to accomlish this task.

author: human-y1
review_text: The reviewer acknowledges the project's innovation in leveraging metagenomic data with AI/ML for protein adaptation studies. rephrased_review: The reviewer acknowledges the project's innovation in leveraging metagenomic data with AI/ML for protein adaptation studies. However, significant concerns exist regarding the validation of the computational pipeline's accuracy and the oversimplification of adaptation mechanisms. The feasibility of the proposed output within the timeline is also questioned.
strengths: The project demonstrates novelty by integrating metagenomic datasets with protein structure/biophysical property prediction and AI/ML for evolutionary insights. The complex interplay of factors in protein sequence evolution is recognized as an emergent phenomenon.
weakness: A major concern is the lack of proposed validation for the computational pipeline, raising issues of error propagation and accuracy in predicting biophysical properties. The proposal also appears to overstate its goals regarding uncovering molecular principles of adaptation, making strong assumptions about conserved function and neglecting potential compensatory effects. Furthermore, the absence of proposed methods to detect signatures of selection is noted.
original_review_text:
[Scientific Merit and Innovation | Score: 3.0]
Strengths: 
1. The evolution of protein sequences to adapt to environmental  conditions involves the complicated interplay of many biophysical,  genetic, and evolutionary processes and is clearly an emergent  phenomenon involving molecular/cellular processes. 
2. Novelty in 1) leveraging metagenomic datasets in which  sequence distributions potentially vary with environmental  conditions, 2) coupling these DNA sequence data with protein  structure/biophysical property prediction, and 3) using AI/ML to  gain insights. 
Weaknesses: 
1. The approach suffers from the "house of cards" problem. While  the individual prediction algorithms such as AlphaFold3 or MD are  very impressive, they are not perfect. But more importantly  predictions from one algorithm, such as AlphaFold3 are fed into  another, such as Metapredict, whose output is fed into a third, such  as ALBATROSS or MD, and so on. The errors would propagate and  potentially amplify and it would be important characterize the  overall accuracy of the algorithm in predicting biophysical  properties of the proteins. Given that these proposals are limited to  computational work, this can be accomplished by applying this  pipeline for proteins whose structure/domains/biophysical  properties have been previously empirically characterized ("ground  truth") and determining the success rate. No such validation of the  proposed pipeline has been proposed. 2. The proposal is overselling its goals. Activity 3 aims to "uncover  the molecular principles governing adaptation of IDRs to diverse  environmental conditions." It appears that the study assumes that  that function would be conserved across environmental conditions  and evolutionary time. This is too strong an assumption.  Phenotypes could be conserved (or not) even if the individual  proteins have different biophysical properties in the different  environmental conditions by compensatory effects in other  processes, such as gene regulation or the function of other  proteins. Evolutionary capacitors, for example, are known to buffer  environmental insults.  
3. In the absence of empirical data about function or selection, one  could potentially use population genetic signatures of selection  (McDonald-Kreitman test etc) to determine whether the IDRs were  evolving or not if it were possible to cluster conspecific sequences.  But no such approach has been proposed. 
Miscellaneous: This project could be considered mesoscale or not  depending on whether the properties of individual proteins are  considered mesoscale

[Feasibility | Score: 4.0]
It is proposed that 4 papers, representing the creation  of an IDR database of 52K proteins, and 400K MD simulations,  multiple AI/ML approaches, would be produced in a 24-month  timeline. While a large team has been assembled, the scope seems  to be on the edge of feasbility, especially since each aim depends  on the previous one.

[Data Sources and Limitations | Score: 5.0]
The project would synthesize information primarily  within the Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0 metagenomic dataset but also the  datasets implicit in the training of the various AI/ML models being  utilized. The data sources are explicitly identified.

[Open Science Compliance | Score: 5.0]
Commitment to team: yes. Commitment to open and  reproducible science principles: nothing explicit has been stated  about data/code sharing and reproducibility (publishing software  containers etc).

[Overall Rating | Score: 3.0]
This is an innovative and important project that fits  NCEMS's remit. However it has the moderate weaknesses of not  proposing any method to characterize the accuracy of the pipeline  in predicting biophysical properties and not really addressing the  question of adaptation raised in activity 3.

This omission raises doubts about the reliability of the project's outcomes.
strengths: The proposal is highly innovative, employing cutting-edge methods and an exciting, untapped dataset to investigate environmental adaptation of IDRs. The investigator team possesses considerable expertise in IDRs and biomolecular condensates.
weakness: A major weakness is the proposal's failure to account for the significant impact of hydrostatic pressure on protein structure and function. Predictive models used for IDR identification are trained on room-pressure structures and are not validated for pressure effects, potentially leading to inaccurate predictions and spurious conclusions for the entire project. The lack of validated coarse-grained models for pressure simulations further exacerbates this issue.
original_review_text:
[Scientific Merit and Innovation | Score: Not provided]
The proposed work could be truly transformational except for one major weakness: pressure. The investigators seem to be entirely ignoring the massive impact that the varying pressure of the ocean has on protein structure/function, a factor that we are only beginning to understand. The predictive models that will be the first step in their identification of IDRs have all been trained on room-pressure structures. We simply don't know enough about pressure as a thermodynamic contributor to protein structure/function for the predictions to be reliable. What we do know is that pressure tends to eliminate void space (see works of Roche and Royer) and that the lone extensive analysis of pressure effects on a proteome (see Moran PRX Life 2024) showed that there are significant structural rearrangements of proteins in response to pressure, broadly speaking, not just for IDRs. If the IDR predictions are inaccurate, then ALL of the work that follows will lead to spurious conclusions. In fact, the applicants admit that they can't include pressure in the simulation work due to the lack of validated CG models. I'm surprised that they feel confident in ESMFold or AlphaFold3's ability to accurately predict disorder for proteins that have evolved to handle high pressure. Great ideas in this proposal, but this fundamental weakness means that the entire project and all the resources dedicated to it may lead to conclusions, models, etc. that are just flat-out wrong.

[Feasibility | Score: Not provided]
Assessing how realistic the timeframe is for the proposed work is outside my expertise. The goals seem appropriate and the timeline is well-described.

[Data Sources and Limitations | Score: Not provided]
The synthesis power of the proposed work seems very strong to me (with the misgivings noted above), and the data set seems an ideal one for the proposed insights.

[Open Science Compliance | Score: Not provided]
This is not explicitly addressed, and I lack the expertise to assess this aspect based simply on reading the methodology proposed. All that is said about dissemination is that they will publish findings. Nothing about making the tools developed or data (structure predictions, trajectories, analytical outputs, etc.) broadly available or anything like that.

[Overall Rating | Score: Not provided]
This proposal aims to unveil environmental adaptation of IDRs from genetic data of marine organisms sample from a broad range of environments. This is an ambitious aim, and the combination of methods proposed is cutting-edge. The investigator team has considerable expertise in IDRs, especially with respect to biomolecular condensates. The data set is an untapped resource for understanding protein structure/function, so that aspect of the proposal is quite exciting. There are several weaknesses, unfortunately, that drive my major skepticism for the reliability of the insights that would result from the proposed work. Most importantly, the proposal fails to recognize the massively complicating factor that pressure will play in the data set, the scientific questions posed, and the methods they propose to use. They don’t plan to simulate pressure due to the absence of a pressure-validated course-grained model, yet they fail to realize that the algorithms they will use to predict intrinsic disorder in the first place are not parameterized in any way to account for the pressure effects on protein structure. The IDR prediction from genetic data is the first step in the entire project, so even a moderate error in that prediction will likely cascade into a host of spurious outputs. I would feel a little bit better about a protein-based analysis of this data set if the goal were to study well-structured proteins with high homology, as there is at least ample data for comparision of well-folded proteins from extremophiles in the PDB, but the plan to examin IDRs, for which the predictive models should not be trusted for extremophilic proteins, is especially worrisome to me.

The work is scientifically important and has the potential to significantly advance knowledge by providing an orthogonal perspective to existing PPI databases. While the overall methodology is sound, specific details for certain activities require further development to ensure clarity and feasibility.
strengths: The project leverages publicly available XL-MS data and integrates structural insights, offering a novel approach to PPI discovery that complements existing methods. The plan to re-analyze and re-post data to meet current quality standards and contribute to the Complex Portal is a valuable contribution to open science. The expertise of the working group leads in relevant databases enhances the feasibility of data curation.
weakness: Methodological details for Activities B and C are not sufficiently described, particularly regarding the assessment of structural models against XL-MS data and the specific outcomes of Activity C. The feasibility of analyzing a large number of structural predictions within the allotted timeframe is unclear, and the anticipated final number of pairs to investigate is not provided.
original_review_text:
[Scientific Merit and Innovation | Score: Not provided]
The proposal does not explicitly discuss the emergent nature of the research, though it can be inferred that the work will uncover protein-protein interactions that are otherwise undetectable when considering data collected differently (i.e. AP-MS). The innovation is to leverage structural insights from both crosslinking MS and structural predictions to describe PPIs in humans and yeast, and to compare the results to the robust PPI landscape that does not consider structural data. This work is important and has great potential to advance knowledge. For the most part, the methodology is clear, logical, and grounded in established research practices. Methodologies for Activities C and, to a lesser extent B, are not described at the same level of detail as Activity A and could be strengthened.

[Feasibility | Score: Not provided]
The researchers have allotted 6 months for NCEMS-assisted manual data curation of publicly available XL-MS data, which seems realistic given that one of the working group leads has expertise with the PRIDE database. The second phase of the project builds upon the first phase to bring in structural predictions as a validation metric. It is unclear if 6 months will be sufficient time to perform and analyze up to 15,000 pairwise structural predictions and the researchers have not provided what they anticipate will be the final number of pairs to investigate. Insufficient methodological detail was supplied to assess if 3 months is realistic to achieve Activity C.

[Data Sources and Limitations | Score: Not provided]
The project is clearly a synthesis effort and will draw from at least 31 publicly available XL-MS datasets describing a total of 6480 total MS experiments. The effort to wrangle this data, curate the metadata, and re-analyze with modern tools is worthwhile. The researchers have identified the datasets clearly and have described the challenges to working with these datasets without manual curation, clearly indicating the need for NCEMS support.

[Open Science Compliance | Score: Not provided]
The researchers will use publicly available data, clean it up and re-analyze, and repost the improved result. This is a great effort to support open, team, reproducible science.

[Overall Rating | Score: Not provided]
The proposed work seeks to uncover protien-protein interactions in humans and yeast using publicly available cross-linking MS data, and to compare the resulting cross-linked peptide hits to structural models of the parental proteins. This work complements existing human PPI networks well as the current methods do not consider structural data and largely rely on affinity-purification MS. The existing PPI data thus may have a high rate of both false positives (lots of "sticky" proteins come down in an AP-MS experiment) and missing interactions (i.e. those that fall apart during purification). XL-MS provides an orthogonal approach, and the researchers use of protein structural predictions to validate their results is compelling. The researchers plan to re-analyze and re-post data to meet current quality standards is valuable, and the goal to incorporate all data into the Complex Portal is good. 

The proposal could be considerably strengthened by further development of Activities B and especially C. For example, specific details on how the researchers will assess the structural models for compatibility with the XL-MS data would be appreciated (Activity B). Even better would be to also utilize existing experimental structure data, which is likely to be available for a large number of human proteins and complexes. Collecting this structural data is a task that NCEMS support could also be used for. Activity C is only very briefly described and it is not very clear what the method or outcome will be. This area merits further deveopment, however it is a minor goal compared to those in Activities A and B.

original_review_text:
[Scientific Merit and Innovation | Score: 4.0]
The evolutionary origin of complex protein
topologies (knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, etc.) is an
understudied phenomenon, and its investigation merits support
as this may reveal previously unappreciated phenomena in the
field of protein structure/function. However, there exists the
possibility that such complex topologies do not have any specific
functional consequences. That is, they may have occurred in the
course of protein evolution and have been carried along, not
because they conferred any special function or benefit, but
simply because they were not detrimental to organismal
survival. It is not clear from the proposal to what extent this
latter scenario may be a possibility and how it would be
incorporated into the scope of the proposal.

[Feasibility | Score: 4]
The proposal anticipates two publications over the
course of the 24-month project timeline. This appears to be an
attainable goal within the timeframe and resources of the
project

[Data Sources and Limitations | Score: 3]
It is unclear to what extent the project will rely on
experimentally determined topologies versus purely
computationally predicted topologies. In the case of
computationally predicted topologies, it is unclear to what
extent errors in computational prediction are likely and how
much those errors might affect the planned work, especially if
the errors are not easily detectable.

[Open Science Compliance | Score: 5.0]
No concerns

[Overall Rating | Score: 4.0]
A key strength of the proposal is the synthesis of
existing databases to probe the evolutionary origin of complex
protein topologies, which is a relatively understudied
phenomenon. The project participants cover a wide range of
topics in science and mathematics that are relevant to the
project. A compelling plan for productive management and
synthesis of this expertise is lacking, including what specific
contributions from NCEMS staff will augment the capacity of the
team. It is not clear what the implications to the project goals are
if complex topologies do not generally have specific functional
consequences. The reliance on computationally predicted
structures increases the overall level of risk.

original_review_text:
[Scientific Merit and Innovation | Score: 3.0]
This proposal directly addresses emergent phenomena by studying inter-organ cross talks at the whole-organism level and proposing to identify organ-specific emergent properties. The PIs propose to implement a reaction-diffusion model based neural network, which is highly innovative. If successful, this can provide a new system-level physiological understanding and advance the field. The proposed generation of digital “twin rat” is also highly innovative, as it could establish a new in silico testbed. While the mathematical framework of the methodology is clear, the proposal lacks some key methodological details. Specifically, the PIs did not explain how the initial graph structure representing organ-to-organ connectivity will be determined, what strategies will ensure comparability across seven different omic layers, and what validation metrics will be used to assess model accuracy and biological relevance.

[Feasibility | Score: 4]
Year 1 goals are achievable, but completing the full 18-organ interaction map by end of Year 2 seems overly ambitious given the complexity of integrating seven omic layers.

[Data Sources and Limitations | Score: 3]
The proposal clearly demonstrates a synthesis project, using the publicly available MoTrPAC dataset. This dataset is sufficient to carry out the proposed activities, as it contains multi omic measurements from 18 tissues across multiple time points from the same animals. The proposal appropriately identifies that using homogeneous data from the same animals addresses a major limitation of previous studies that relied on heterogeneous datasets. However, the proposal does not discuss potential limitations such as missing data across omic types, varying measurement frequencies, data quality issues, or batch effects.

[Open Science Compliance | Score: 2.0]
There is no explicit statement regarding open science principles. No plans for data sharing, code repositories, or reproducibility frameworks were mentioned.
